description:
Helena never imagined that accepting an urban revitalization project would bring her so close to Alexander Blackwood, a man as controlled as he is irresistible, with whom her relationship begins marked by conflict, distrust, and an attraction impossible to ignore. As they try to work together, old documents, anonymous messages, photographs, and secrets involving the Blackwood and Morgan families reveal a history of manipulation, broken loyalties, and an accident that has remained unexplained for fifteen years.

As the truth comes to light, Helena and Alexander must decide whether they can put their pride aside and trust each other. Between painful discoveries, threats, and feelings that can no longer be hidden, they finally confront the past and find the freedom to choose the future they want to build together.

chapters.title: First Impressions
chapters.content:
Helena had always believed that first impressions were dangerous. Not because they were necessarily wrong, but because they had the unfortunate habit of turning into certainties before there was enough time to discover the truth. Even so, that afternoon, as she crossed the marble lobby of the Blackwood building, the sound of her own footsteps echoing discreetly between the glass and metal walls, she had the uncomfortable feeling that some people really could reveal a great deal about themselves within the first five minutes. Maybe it was simply nervousness. Maybe it was the environment. Or maybe it was the man who was about to enter her life without her having the slightest idea how much space he would eventually occupy in it.

The building seemed designed to remind anyone who entered exactly where they stood in the hierarchy of the world. Everything was too large, too flawless, too quiet. The pale marble floor reflected the golden light coming through the enormous windows, fresh flower arrangements occupied strategic points throughout the space, and the employees moved with almost choreographed discretion, dressed in elegant clothes and carrying tablets or folders that seemed as important as the people holding them. Helena adjusted the strap of her bag on her shoulder and tried to ignore the feeling that her simple beige coat and flat shoes belonged to another universe. It wasn't insecurity. At least that was what she kept telling herself. She knew what she did, she knew why she was there, and above all, she knew she didn't need to impress anyone.

Still, when the receptionist confirmed her name and asked her to wait, Helena felt a small knot in her stomach.

“Ms. Helena Duarte?”

“Yes.”

“Mr. Blackwood is expecting you.”

Helena raised her eyebrows slightly.

“He is?”

The woman smiled professionally.

“Yes. He asked me to send you directly to him as soon as you arrived.”

That was curious. The man Helena was about to meet had a reputation that had reached her long before this encounter. Alexander Blackwood, in his early thirties, was the leading name of the new generation of the family that had built one of the largest business groups in the country. His name appeared in business magazines, newspapers, interviews and, occasionally, photographs beside models, actresses, or heiresses from families as wealthy as his own. Helena had never paid much attention to any of it. Not because she didn't know who he was, but because she had learned early in life that money said absolutely nothing about someone's character.

She thanked the receptionist and followed the indicated corridor. As she walked, the silence of the place seemed even more noticeable. There were no loud conversations, laughter, or the usual noise of busy offices. Everything seemed carefully controlled, as if even the air had been given instructions about how it should move. Helena passed a glass wall revealing an empty meeting room and, a few meters later, stopped in front of a dark door.

She knocked twice.

There was no answer.

She waited a few seconds and knocked again.

Still nothing.

Helena looked at her watch.

Ten minutes earlier, she had arrived exactly at the agreed time. She disliked delays and, above all, disliked being kept waiting. She considered leaving for approximately three seconds before taking a deep breath and opening the door.

That was when she saw him.

Alexander Blackwood stood with his back to her, facing the windows that occupied practically the entire wall of the office. The city stretched out below him, distant and small, while the man remained motionless, one hand in the pocket of his dark trousers and the other holding a phone. He wore a perfectly tailored black suit, no tie, with the first button of his white shirt undone. There was something about him that immediately caught Helena's attention, although she couldn't yet say exactly what.

Perhaps it was his calm.

Perhaps it was the posture of someone accustomed to being watched without needing to look at anyone.

Or perhaps it was simply the fact that he had made her wait while continuing to stare out the window as though the rest of the world could wait.

“Mr. Blackwood?”

He ended the call before turning around.

And Helena understood, in that instant, why so many photographs of him seemed incapable of fully capturing his presence.

Alexander was more impressive in person.

He had dark hair, slightly tousled in a way that probably required more effort than it should have, light eyes, and an expression that revealed absolutely nothing. He wasn't exactly handsome in the conventional, carefully produced way of magazine covers. There was something more unsettling about him. A confidence that bordered on arrogance, a calmness that made it seem as though he was rarely surprised, and a gaze that lingered a few seconds longer than necessary on Helena.

He looked her up and down before returning his gaze to her face.

Helena felt a stab of irritation but kept her expression neutral.

“Ms. Duarte.”

His voice was low and firm.

“Yes.”

“You're late.”

She blinked, incredulous.

She looked at the clock.

“Actually, I believe I arrived a few minutes before the agreed time.”

Alexander cast a quick glance at the clock on the desk.

“You're right.”

Helena waited for something that never came.

An apology, perhaps.

He simply pointed to the chair in front of the desk.

“Sit.”

It was at that moment that Helena decided she would need quite a lot of patience with him.

It wasn't a definitive conclusion, obviously. She didn't know him yet. But some people had a particular talent for making a first impression extremely memorable.

She walked to the chair and sat without answering. Alexander took the seat behind the desk and opened a folder lying in front of him. Helena noticed that he didn't ask whether she wanted water or coffee, made no polite comment, and didn't even try to begin a conventional conversation. He simply started reading the documents as though she were another item on an extremely full agenda.

“Do you know why you're here?” he asked after a few seconds.

Helena folded her hands in her lap.

“I was informed that the Blackwood Group is evaluating a new proposal for the revitalization of the historic district and that my team was selected to present an independent analysis.”

“Your team?”

“Duarte & Associates.”

“I know it.”

She tilted her head slightly.

“I'm pleased to hear that.”

Alexander looked up.

“Was that sarcasm?”

“No. I simply considered it positive information for the progress of the project.”

“It sounded like it.”

“Perhaps it was the way I expressed myself.”

Alexander closed the folder.

“You were recommended by people I trust.”

“I appreciate the confidence placed in our work.”

“That is the only reason you're here.”

Helena maintained her calm posture.

“I hope our competence will also be a sufficient reason for us to remain.”

He watched her for several seconds.

“Interesting.”

“May I ask what you find interesting?”

“You.”

Helena hadn't expected that answer. Even so, she didn't allow her surprise to show on her face.

“I hope that's positive for the project.”

“I'm still deciding.”

She breathed discreetly.

“In that case, I hope I'll have the opportunity to help you make a favorable decision.”

For several seconds, Alexander said nothing. Then he stood.

Helena followed the movement with her eyes.

“Come with me.”

“Where?”

“I want to show you something.”

“Certainly.”

She closed the folder and stood. Alexander opened the door.

“Are you coming?”

“Yes.”

He walked down the corridor, and Helena followed. After a few steps, she realized she had no idea where they were going.

“May I ask where we're going?”

“I want to show you the project site.”

“I understand.”

The short answer seemed to satisfy him.

As they walked, Helena noticed that Alexander received discreet greetings from practically every employee they passed. Some stopped to ask quick questions, while others simply greeted him with a respectful nod. He answered everyone with a few words, but he never seemed uncertain about what he should say. There was a natural authority in the way he occupied spaces that Helena couldn't deny.

Maybe it was a quality acquired over the years.

Maybe it was simply the surname.

She preferred not to decide.

When they reached the lower floor, Alexander swiped a card through the access door and led her into a room where plans, maps, and images of the historic district were spread across a large table.

“This is the project,” he said.

Helena stepped closer.

Over the next few minutes, she completely forgot the first impression she had formed of him. Not because Alexander had changed, but because she realized that behind his controlled demeanor and almost authoritarian way of conducting the meeting was a man who knew the project he was responsible for inside and out. He knew every detail, remembered numbers, contracts, names, and dates, asked specific questions, and quickly identified the weak points in any argument.

Helena didn't like admitting it.

She liked it even less when he asked a question to which she didn't have an immediate answer.

“What is the projected economic impact on local businesses during the first two years?” he asked.

Helena opened her folder.

“We have a preliminary estimate, but we're still consolidating some data before presenting a definitive projection.”

“Preliminary?”

“Yes.”

“So you came to present an incomplete analysis?”

Helena looked up.

“I came to present an analysis in development. There is a difference.”

“For me, the difference is small.”

“I understand your concern, but I would rather present a responsible projection than provide a number simply to fill a gap.”

Alexander placed his hands on the table.

“Do you always answer like that when you don't have information?”

Helena kept her tone calm.

“When I don't have information, I prefer to admit that I don't have it yet. I believe that's more appropriate in a professional analysis.”

He remained silent for a few seconds.

Then he nodded.

“Finally, an honest answer.”

Helena slowly closed the folder.

“I believe transparency is important for a project of this scale.”

“I agree.”

It was a simple answer, but Helena noticed that something had changed in his expression.

Alexander walked toward the window.

“No one usually tells me that.”

“Maybe because many people confuse respect with agreement.”

He turned.

Their eyes met.

For some reason, this time neither of them said anything.

Helena felt a kind of silent tension forming in the space between them. It wasn't exactly uncomfortable. It was worse. It was a strange, unexpected sensation that she didn't want to name because any name she gave it would be absurd.

Alexander looked away first.

“We're done for today.”

“Okay.”

“Tomorrow, at nine.”

Helena gathered the documents.

“Tomorrow?”

“Yes.”

“I didn't know there would be another meeting.”

“The project starts tomorrow.”

She closed the folder.

“I understand. In that case, I'll check my schedule and confirm the time with your assistant.”

Alexander stared at her for a moment.

“At nine.”

Helena held his gaze.

“I'll do my best to be here at nine.”

“Don't do your best. Be here.”

She could have answered in several ways.

She chose the most professional one.

“I'll be here.”

Alexander seemed satisfied.

“Good.”

Helena walked toward the door.

“Good afternoon, Mr. Blackwood.”

“Helena.”

She stopped.

It was the first time he had said her name.

She looked back.

Alexander was standing in the middle of the room, his hands in his pockets, his face serious again.

“See you tomorrow.”

Helena nodded.

“See you tomorrow.”

And she left.

In the hallway, Helena released the breath she hadn't realized she had been holding.

She walked toward the elevator, trying to organize her thoughts, but one thing kept returning to her mind.

His gaze.

That calm, attentive gaze that seemed to notice more than it revealed.

She pressed the elevator button and watched the numbers slowly descend on the panel.

There was no reason to think too much about that encounter. Alexander Blackwood was simply the person responsible for the project, an extremely wealthy man accustomed to running major businesses and, apparently, unaccustomed to hearing opinions different from his own.

That was all. The elevator arrived, the doors opened, and Helena stepped inside.

chapters.title: Work Routine
chapters.content:
The next morning, Helena arrived at the Blackwood building eight minutes before the agreed time, even though she had promised herself while getting ready that she would not allow Alexander Blackwood to dictate even the pace of her routine. Still, there was something ironic about realizing that, from the moment she had opened her eyes, that meeting had occupied a considerable part of her thoughts. Not because she was looking forward to seeing him—at least that was what she told herself—but because the conversation the day before had left an impression that was difficult to ignore. Alexander had a particular way of handling people, as if he were constantly several steps ahead of every situation, and Helena didn't like the feeling of not knowing exactly what he was thinking. There were men who imposed themselves through their voices, others through their money, others through their need to be admired. Alexander seemed to need none of those things. He only had to enter a room and, somehow, the atmosphere reorganized itself around him.

She crossed the marble lobby again, this time without the same hesitation as the day before. She already knew the way, recognized some of the employees, and didn't need to wait for the receptionist to know where she was supposed to go. Still, as she approached the elevators, she noticed that one of the doors was about to close. She quickened her pace, reached out, and managed to stop the doors from closing.

“Sorry.”

The person inside looked up.

Alexander.

For a moment, neither of them said anything.

Helena stepped into the elevator.

“Good morning, Mr. Blackwood.”

“Good morning.”

The doors closed.

She pressed the button for the floor and kept her eyes fixed on the numbers appearing on the panel. Alexander stood beside her, close enough that she couldn't help noticing his presence, but far enough away for it to be considered nothing more than a coincidence. The silence between them wasn't exactly uncomfortable. It was simply strange. Perhaps because they both seemed too aware of the other's presence.

“Punctual,” he remarked.

Helena turned her head slightly.

“I try to be.”

“Yesterday you said you'd do your best.”

“And today I'm here.”

“I noticed.”

She almost smiled.

“Then I believe the timing is satisfactory.”

Alexander looked at her.

“It is.”

The elevator continued upward.

Helena looked forward again, but she noticed through the metallic reflection of the doors that he was still watching her. She didn't ask why. She had no intention of turning every gesture from that man into some kind of hidden meaning. Maybe he was simply looking at her. People looked at one another. There was nothing extraordinary about that.

When the doors opened, Alexander made a small gesture for her to exit first.

“After you.”

Helena looked at him for a second.

“Thank you.”

She stepped out.

They walked side by side down the corridor. For the first time, Helena realized that Alexander's silence wasn't necessarily coldness. Maybe it was simply part of who he was. He seemed to save his words, as if every sentence needed to serve a specific purpose. It was almost the opposite of her, having learned over the years that a professional conversation didn't need to be excessively formal to be effective.

When they reached the meeting room, Helena found a series of documents arranged in small stacks on the table, accompanied by an open laptop and two cups of coffee. One of them was in front of the chair she had occupied the day before.

She looked at the cup.

Then at Alexander.

“Coffee?”

“Black. No sugar.”

Helena frowned slightly.

“How do you know?”

He pulled out a chair.

“Yesterday you ordered one when you arrived at the building.”

She didn't remember mentioning that to him.

“You pay attention to details.”

“It is part of my job.”

Helena picked up the cup.

“Thank you.”

She sat down.

Alexander took the chair opposite her.

For a few seconds, the meeting seemed to begin perfectly normally. They reviewed documents, discussed deadlines, analyzed projections, and went over the points that needed to be adjusted. Helena quickly realized that working with Alexander would be more demanding than she had imagined. He didn't accept vague answers, disliked estimates without justification, and asked questions that forced Helena to mentally review every assumption used by the team.

On the other hand, he also listened.

That was something she hadn't expected.

When Helena disagreed with a decision, Alexander didn't simply end the discussion because he had the authority to do so. He asked why. He wanted data, arguments, consequences. And when the reasoning was sound, he was willing to reconsider.

That bothered her more than it should have.

It would have been much easier not to like him if Alexander were simply arrogant.

The problem was that behind that controlled demeanor and that surname that seemed to open every door, there was someone competent.

Very competent.

“I don't agree with this part,” Helena said, pointing to a section of the document.

Alexander looked up.

“Why?”

“Because we're only considering the direct economic impact. If the goal is to revitalize the area, we need to include the indirect effects on small businesses. The flow of people could completely change the local dynamic, and that doesn't appear in this projection.”

He leaned over the table.

“You believe the indirect impact will be greater?”

“I believe it could be. But we need more data to state that with certainty.”

“How long?”

“Two days.”

Alexander was silent.

“One.”

Helena stared at him.

“Two.”

“One and a half.”

“Two.”

He held her gaze for several seconds.

“One and a half days.”

Helena took a deep breath.

“All right.”

A small smile appeared on his face.

“I knew we'd reach an agreement.”

“Don't confuse negotiation with victory.”

“I don't.”

She returned to the documents.

“Good.”

The meeting continued for more than an hour, until one of the group's directors entered the room without knocking. She was an elegant woman, probably a little older than Alexander, wearing a navy-blue dress and carrying a tablet in her hands. She stopped when she realized Helena was there.

“Alexander, I needed to speak with you about the London meeting.”

“Not now, Claire.”

The woman looked at Helena.

“Of course.”

She didn't leave immediately.

Alexander looked up.

“Is there a problem?”

“No. I just needed to confirm a detail on the schedule.”

“We'll talk later.”

Claire nodded.

“Of course.”

She turned and left.

Helena returned her eyes to the documents, trying not to show any interest in the conversation. She had no reason to pay attention. Still, she noticed that Alexander was continuing to look at her.

“Something wrong?” she asked.

“You went quiet.”

“We were working.”

“You usually have some observation.”

Helena smiled faintly.

“Maybe I'm learning to choose my battles.”

“With me?”

“In general.”

Alexander leaned back in his chair.

“And is it working?”

“I'm still evaluating.”

He let out a low laugh.

Helena returned to reading the documents. The conversation had ended, but the small moment remained somewhere in her awareness, not exactly because of Claire's presence, but because of the way Alexander always seemed to notice when she was paying attention to something.

She preferred not to think too much about it.

The rest of the meeting passed without further incident. When they finished, Helena carefully organized the documents, checked some notes, and placed everything in her folder. Alexander did the same on the other side of the table.

“Will the data update be ready tomorrow?” he asked.

“I believe so. My team has already started working on it.”

“Good.”

“As soon as it's completed, I'll send it directly to your team.”

“You can send it to me.”

Helena looked up.

“Directly to you?”

“To me.”

She nodded.

“All right.”

Alexander stood.

“And Helena?”

She stopped as she closed her bag.

“Yes?”

“Yesterday's report was very good.”

The statement surprised her more than it should have.

“Thank you.”

“You only need to revise the section about the local businesses.”

“I was already considering that.”

“I imagined you were.”

Helena placed the bag over her shoulder.

“Then we're in agreement.”

“Seems so.”

She walked toward the door.

“See you tomorrow, Mr. Blackwood.”

“See you tomorrow.”

When she left the room, Helena realized that the compliment was still in her mind.

It wasn't exactly unusual to receive recognition for her work. She was used to it. Still, there was something different about the way Alexander had said it. It didn't sound like an attempt to please her or a business formality. He had genuinely analyzed her work and reached that conclusion.

And for some reason, that made her happy.

---

That evening, Helena was at home when Sofia showed up at the apartment without warning, carrying two bags of food and an expression that made it clear she had no intention of accepting any excuse to be sent away.

“Before you say anything, I brought dinner.”

Helena stepped aside to let her in.

“You could have warned me.”

“If I had, you'd probably say you were busy.”

“I am busy.”

Sofia left the bags on the counter.

“Exactly.”

Helena smiled.

“The project is demanding a lot.”

“And the man?”

Helena gave her friend a look.

“The man is demanding too.”

Sofia laughed.

“So you two got along.”

“I wouldn't say that.”

“Did you fight?”

“No.”

“Disagree?”

“A few times.”

“Then everything is normal.”

Helena opened one of the containers.

“He's very detail-oriented.”

“Is that bad?”

“Not necessarily. Actually, he knows the project very well. I expected him to be more dependent on the team, considering the size of the company, but he's not.”

Sofia rested her elbow on the counter.

“So he's competent.”

“Yes.”

“And rich.”

Helena sighed.

“Very.”

“Handsome?”

Helena took a moment before answering.

“Sofia.”

“What? I'm just asking.”

“You've seen pictures of him.”

“Pictures don't count.”

Helena picked up a fork.

“Yes. He's handsome.”

Sofia smiled.

“Finally, some interesting information.”

“There is nothing interesting about that.”

“Of course.”

Helena pointed the fork at her.

“He's a client.”

“I know.”

“And I'm working.”

“I know that too.”

“So don't turn a professional situation into something it isn't.”

Sofia raised her hands.

“All right. I won't.”

Helena nodded and returned to her food.

For a few seconds, the two of them remained silent.

Then Sofia asked:

“And do you like the project?”

Helena thought for a moment.

“Yes. I think it could be important work.”

“Then everything's fine.”

Helena smiled.

“It is.”

And for the first time since she had started working with the Blackwoods, she realized that this was exactly how she wanted things to remain: simple, professional, and focused on the work.

---

The next morning, Helena arrived at the Blackwood office again.

This time, however, Alexander wasn't in the meeting room.

His assistant informed her that he had been called into an urgent meeting and asked her to wait.

She sat down.

Five minutes.

Ten.

Twenty.

When she was about to open her laptop, she heard voices in the hallway.

“We can't simply postpone this again.”

Alexander's voice.

“I know.”

Another man's voice answered.

“Then you need to decide.”

Helena hadn't intended to listen.

In fact, she wasn't trying to listen.

But the door to the room was slightly open and the voices were getting closer.

“I'm not going to make a decision this way.”

“Your father expected you to have done it already.”

Silence.

Helena looked up.

The Blackwood name seemed to carry much more weight than she had imagined.

The man's voice continued:

“You know what's at stake.”

“I know.”

“Then stop acting as if you have all the time in the world.”

Footsteps.

Helena quickly returned her attention to the laptop.

The door opened.

Alexander entered alone.

His face was different.

Not much.

But enough.

The usual expression of control seemed to have been replaced by something more closed off, more distant. He noticed Helena immediately and stopped for a moment.

“You're early.”

“A few minutes.”

Alexander nodded.

“Sorry to keep you waiting.”

Helena closed the laptop.

“No problem.”

He walked to the table.

“We can start.”

Helena watched him for a moment.

“Is everything all right?”

Alexander looked up.

“Yes.”

It was too quick an answer.

She could have insisted.

She didn't.

“All right.”

He sat down.

For the next few minutes, they worked normally, but something had changed. Alexander seemed more distracted, answered questions with fewer details, and at times remained staring at the documents without actually reading them.

Helena noticed.

And although she knew it wasn't her place, she ended up asking:

“If you need to reschedule, we can continue another day.”

He looked up.

“No.”

“All right.”

“I want to finish this today.”

“Okay.”

She returned to work.

After a few minutes, Alexander spoke.

“My father is ill.”

Helena stopped.

He continued looking at the document.

“You don't need to say anything. I just thought I should explain why I'm a little distracted.”

Helena closed her pen.

“I'm sorry.”

Alexander nodded.

“Thank you.”

That was all.

That small revelation changed something.

Not because Helena knew what to do with the information, but because, for the first time, she saw a crack in the flawless image he presented to the world.

Alexander didn't seem invincible.

He simply seemed like someone trying not to show that he was worried.

And that made Helena see him differently.

The meeting ended earlier that day. Helena put the documents away and checked her notes again before standing.

“The updated report will be ready tomorrow,” she said.

Alexander nodded.

“I know.”

She placed her bag over her shoulder.

“Then, see you tomorrow.”

“See you tomorrow.”

Helena walked toward the door.

“Helena.”

She turned.

“Yes?”

Alexander remained silent for a moment, as though he had thought about saying something and decided not to.

“Thank you for today.”

She smiled faintly.

“You don't need to thank me. It's my job.”

“I know.”

Helena nodded.

“Good night, Alexander.”

He looked up when he heard his own name.

For a brief moment, neither of them said anything.

Then he replied:

“Good night, Helena.”

She left the room and closed the door behind her.

In the hallway, she slowed her pace for a few seconds, feeling a strange urge to look back.

She didn't.

She continued to the elevator, pressed the button, and when the doors opened, stepped inside alone.

As she descended, she opened the folder and checked the project documents again, focusing on the numbers and notes she would need to review that evening. It was easier to think about work.

And, for now, that was exactly what she intended to do.

chapters.title: Between Us
chapters.content:
A few weeks were enough to transform Helena's routine in the Blackwood building into something so familiar that she no longer had to think about the way to the meeting room, the times when the elevators were usually emptier, or the black coffee that almost always waited for her on the desk when she arrived. The project moved forward slowly, requiring constant meetings, document reviews, visits to the historic district, and countless hours spent in front of spreadsheets that seemed to multiply every time one of them was completed. What had initially seemed like nothing more than an important assignment had become a considerable part of her days, and Helena already knew some members of the team by name, knew which discussions would probably end in consensus and which would require a second meeting, and had even learned to recognize Alexander's moods through the small details he probably imagined no one noticed. During the first few weeks, he had simply been demanding. Then, he had become predictable in his demands. Over the last few days, however, something had changed.

Alexander was more distant.

It was not an obvious kind of distance, the sort that could be pointed out during a conversation. He was still present when he needed to be, answered messages, attended the most important meetings, and made decisions with the same objectivity as always. But there were moments when he seemed to be physically in a room and mentally somewhere else, especially since his father's illness had become more serious. The calls he received during meetings had increased, as had the number of times he had to leave the building in a hurry or cancel appointments because of some medical update. Helena did not ask questions. She had learned that some people needed space to deal with things they could not fix, and Alexander seemed to belong exactly to that group. Even so, there was something contradictory about the way he behaved. The more distant he became from everyone, the more attentive he seemed to be toward Helena.

That morning, she was in the middle of a presentation when the meeting room door opened and a man Helena had never met entered accompanied by one of the project's directors. He looked to be a little over thirty, perhaps a few years older than her, and had a very different appearance from Alexander's. He did not carry the almost impenetrable formality that seemed to follow every member of the Blackwood family; he wore a light-blue shirt with the sleeves rolled up to his forearms, dark trousers, and no sign that he had spent the morning trying to appear more important than he was. He carried a slim folder under one arm and wore an open, almost relaxed expression that contrasted with the usual seriousness of the room.

"Helena, this is Daniel Morgan," Claire introduced. "He'll be taking over coordination of the social impact and merchant relations side during this phase of the project."

Helena closed the presentation on her laptop and stood.

"It's a pleasure to meet you."

Daniel held out his hand.

"The pleasure is mine. I've heard quite a bit about your work."

"I hope it was good things."

"So far, yes. But I'm still gathering information before forming my own opinion."

Helena laughed softly.

"Fair enough."

Daniel smiled.

"I like working with people who don't try to convince me of something before I have the data."

"Then I think we'll get along."

"We're off to a good start."

Claire watched the two of them for a moment before indicating the empty chair beside Helena.

"Daniel will be working with you during the next stages. He has experience in urban revitalization projects and worked on two similar projects in London."

"And in Lisbon," Daniel added. "But that project almost made me quit the profession."

Helena smiled.

"Then maybe it's better if you don't tell me the details."

"I can tell you during the break."

"I'll consider it."

The conversation continued naturally, and Helena quickly understood why Daniel had been chosen. He did not try to dominate the meeting or show a need to prove that he knew more than everyone else. He asked objective questions, listened to the answers until the end, and seemed genuinely interested in the people who would be affected by the project, not just the numbers that would appear in the reports. When Helena presented the analysis she had prepared on the area's small business owners, Daniel not only agreed with some of her points but also added information that could strengthen the research.

"You considered the impact on the smaller businesses, but you didn't include businesses operating in informally rented properties," he commented, pointing to one of the tables.

Helena leaned closer to look.

"Because we still haven't been able to confirm the numbers."

"I can."

She looked up.

"You can?"

"I have contacts with a merchants' association that works specifically with this kind of survey. I can ask them for the data."

"That would help a lot."

"Then consider it done."

Helena smiled.

"Thank you."

Across the table, Alexander remained silent.

He had arrived a few minutes after the meeting began, apologized for being late, and sat down without making any comments. Since then, he had been watching the presentation while absently rolling a pen between his fingers. Helena had noticed his presence, of course, but she had not paid much attention to him. Over the past few weeks, she had learned to work beside him without letting herself be affected by the way Alexander watched people or by the long pauses that sometimes appeared when they disagreed about something. That morning, however, she noticed that he was looking at Daniel.

It was not exactly a hostile look.

It was simply... too attentive.

"If we can get those figures by Friday, I can cross-reference them with the survey we already have," Helena said.

"I can get them sooner," Daniel replied. "Maybe tomorrow."

"That would be great."

"Tomorrow, then."

"Deal."

Alexander finally set the pen down on the table.

"We don't need to accelerate the schedule because of that."

Helena looked at him.

"We're not accelerating it. We're trying to meet the deadline."

"The deadline remains the same."

Daniel turned to Alexander.

"And the additional data won't affect the deadline. It will just improve the analysis."

Alexander held his gaze for several seconds.

"I know."

The answer was simple, but the tone ended the discussion.

Helena returned to her laptop, although she had noticed the change in the atmosphere. Nothing had happened that could be considered inappropriate. Alexander had simply expressed a concern. It was exactly the kind of thing he did in every meeting. Even so, there was something different about that response, a rigidity that had not been there a few minutes earlier.

When the meeting ended, Claire was the first to leave, followed by Daniel, who stopped beside Helena as she organized the documents.

"Are you having lunch here?"

Helena looked up.

"Probably. I have a few things to finish."

"Then take a break before going back to them."

"Is that an order?"

"A professional suggestion."

She smiled.

"I'll consider it."

"Great. See you tomorrow."

"See you tomorrow."

Daniel left.

Helena went back to putting the documents in her folder and only realized that Alexander was still in the room when she heard the door close behind him. She looked up.

"Aren't you going?"

"In a minute."

"Okay."

She closed her bag.

"Do you need anything?"

"No."

Helena waited for a moment.

"Then I'm going downstairs."

"Daniel is new to the team."

She frowned slightly.

"I know."

"I'm just saying."

"Right."

Alexander rested his hands on the table.

"He's going to be working directly with you."

"Yes."

"That could change some of the priorities we established."

Helena watched him silently for a moment.

"If there's any change in scope, we can discuss it. But from what I understand, he's only going to complement one part of the analysis."

"I know."

"Then I don't see a problem."

Alexander looked away.

"I didn't say there was a problem."

"No."

She put her bag over her shoulder.

"But it sounded like there was."

He looked at her again.

"Are you saying I seem concerned?"

"I'm saying you seem concerned about something."

For a moment, Alexander did not answer. His expression remained controlled, but there was a subtle tension in his jaw.

"My father got worse this week."

The answer immediately softened Helena's tone.

"I'm sorry. I didn't know."

"It doesn't matter."

"It does."

He took a deep breath and ran a hand over his face, a rare gesture that Helena noticed immediately.

"I'm trying to manage a few things at once."

"I can imagine."

"And maybe I'm not doing it very well."

She remained silent for a few seconds.

"You don't have to do everything alone."

Alexander gave a small humorless laugh.

"That's something people say when they don't know what else to say."

"Maybe."

Helena walked toward the door.

"But sometimes it's still true."

Alexander watched her leave.

In the hallway, Helena took a deep breath and headed toward the elevator. She did not know exactly why that conversation had left her with a different feeling. Maybe because, for the first time, Alexander had admitted that he was struggling without trying to turn it into a business matter. Maybe because she had seen something in him that she was not used to seeing: exhaustion. Not the physical exhaustion of someone who worked too much, but that of a person trying to keep an entire life standing while something important was silently falling apart beside him.

Over the following days, Daniel became part of the project's routine with surprising ease. He and Helena worked well together, especially because they had similar ways of conducting discussions. Neither needed to turn a disagreement into a dispute, and there was a lightness to their conversations that made the long hours of work less tiring. Sometimes they would spend nearly an hour discussing a table or an interview with merchants and, at some point, the subject would drift toward something that had nothing to do with the project. Daniel discovered that Helena liked walking without a destination when she had time, that she preferred small cafés to sophisticated restaurants, and that she had an almost inexplicable difficulty saying no to books whenever she entered a bookstore. Helena discovered that he had lived in three different cities, that he hated very early meetings, and that he had a habit of making terrible jokes when he was tired.

It was simple.

Natural.

And perhaps that was exactly what made his company so pleasant.

With Alexander, Helena always had to stay alert. Every conversation seemed to require some kind of balance, as if the two of them were constantly testing each other's limits. With Daniel, there was no competition. There was no need to choose each word carefully. They simply talked.

And Alexander noticed.

The first time, he paid no attention.

The second, he noticed that Daniel made Helena laugh.

The third, it started to bother him.

The fourth, he could no longer pretend he had not noticed.

He was sitting on the other side of the meeting room that afternoon, reviewing a contract while Helena and Daniel discussed some research results. He should not have been paying attention to their conversation. He had enough problems to occupy his mind, especially his father's health, the decisions approaching within the company, and the growing number of responsibilities falling onto his shoulders. Even so, at some point he realized he had not read a single line of the document in the last five minutes.

"Are you listening?" Helena asked.

Alexander looked up.

"Of course."

"Then what was the last thing I said?"

He looked at her.

Silence.

Daniel tried to hide a smile.

Helena crossed her arms.

"I thought so."

Alexander closed the folder.

"I was thinking about something else."

"I noticed."

"Then why did you ask?"

"Because you looked like you were paying attention."

"I was."

"You weren't."

Daniel laughed.

"I think you lost that one."

Alexander shot him a look.

"No one asked for your opinion."

Daniel raised his hands.

"All right."

Helena held back a smile.

"We're talking about the report."

"I know."

"Good."

She returned to her laptop.

Alexander watched her face for a few seconds before returning to his own document. He did not like that feeling. He did not like the way Daniel could make her smile effortlessly, nor the fact that Helena seemed more relaxed when she was around him. It was irrational. There was absolutely nothing wrong with their relationship. Daniel was part of the team. Helena was a professional working on a project. He had no reason to care.

And precisely because of that, he could not understand why he cared so much.

Over the following days, Alexander became more provocative with Helena. Not in a way that could easily be identified by someone who did not know them, but enough for her to begin noticing. He commented on the coffee she always forgot to finish, questioned why she arrived so early, teased her about the number of notes she made in the margins of documents, and occasionally found absurdly specific reasons to challenge one of her choices.

"Do you really need to make so many notes?" he asked one morning, looking at the report she was holding.

"Yes."

"It seems a little excessive."

"It's organization."

"It looks like an obsession."

Helena looked up.

"Are you worried about my organization?"

"I'm trying to understand."

"You don't need to."

"Maybe I want to."

She held his gaze for a moment.

"Then ask."

Alexander seemed to consider the answer.

"Why do you always arrive before everyone else?"

"Because I like to start the day without rushing."

"And why do you work so late?"

"Because I have deadlines."

"You always have an answer."

"You always have a question."

He smiled.

"Maybe."

Helena closed the folder.

"Anything else?"

"No."

"Then I need to get back to work."

"Of course."

She walked away.

Alexander followed her with his eyes until she disappeared down the hallway. Only then did he realize that he had completely forgotten why he had called her over.

The problem was that the more he tried to understand it, the less sense it made.

He was not interested in Helena.

He could not be.

She was his consultant, a competent professional he had been working with for a few weeks. That was it. Nothing more. The fact that she was intelligent, independent, and capable of standing up to him without turning every disagreement into a fight meant nothing. The fact that Daniel seemed to enjoy her company meant nothing either.

Nothing.

Alexander repeated that to himself so many times that he began to suspect the very need to do so.

On Friday, the project required a visit to the historic district. Helena, Daniel, and two members of the team left together after lunch to conduct some interviews with merchants and assess the latest proposed adjustments. Alexander was not supposed to participate. He had a meeting with the company's board and another call with the hospital where his father was staying. But shortly before Helena left the building, he appeared in the lobby.

"You're going to the historic district?" he asked.

She stopped.

"Yes."

"I'm coming with you."

Helena frowned slightly.

"I thought you had a meeting."

"It was postponed."

Daniel appeared behind her.

"Perfect. Then we can show you the latest changes."

Alexander nodded.

"Of course."

The drive was quiet. Daniel and Helena continued talking in the back seat, discussing one of the interviews they would conduct that afternoon. Alexander remained in the front seat, occasionally answering messages on his phone. At one point, he heard Daniel tell a story about an old project and Helena laugh.

He looked in the rearview mirror.

She was smiling.

For some reason, that bothered him.

When they arrived, the work began immediately. Helena spoke with merchants, took notes, photographed a few specific locations, and discussed with Daniel the best way to reorganize the data. Alexander remained nearby, but was quieter than usual. After almost two hours, when they began walking toward a café to review their notes, Daniel lightly touched Helena's arm to get her attention.

"Look at that."

She turned.

"What?"

"The façade. I hadn't noticed that detail before."

Helena moved closer.

"Wow. That changes a few things."

"Exactly."

Alexander watched the two of them.

There was nothing wrong.

Daniel had merely touched her arm.

Helena had merely stepped closer.

Nothing.

Absolutely nothing.

Even so, Alexander felt a sudden, inexplicable irritation.

"We need to go back," he said.

Helena turned to him.

"Now?"

"Yes."

"We still have the café."

"We can review the data at the office."

Daniel looked at Alexander.

"I don't see any need to go back so soon."

"I do."

Helena noticed his tone.

"Alexander, we have two more interviews scheduled."

"Then do them."

"Without you?"

He looked at her.

"You don't need me for that."

The answer was colder than he intended.

Helena remained silent for a few seconds.

"All right."

Daniel looked at her.

"If you want, we can continue."

"Let's go."

Alexander felt something tighten in his chest.

It was not anger.

It was worse.

It was the feeling of losing something he had no right to want.

He took a step back.

"Do whatever you think is best."

He turned before anyone could answer and began walking back toward the car.

Helena watched him for a few seconds.

Daniel noticed.

"He's acting strange."

She looked away.

"He's going through a lot."

"You always find an explanation for him."

Helena did not answer immediately.

"Maybe because I know a little more about him now."

Daniel smiled faintly.

"Maybe."

They continued walking.

Alexander reached the car alone.

He sat in the back seat, closed the door, and spent a few seconds staring out the window. He had spent weeks trying to convince himself that it meant nothing. Now, for the first time, he was beginning to realize that perhaps the problem was not Helena.

It was him.

Later, back at the office, Helena entered his room without knocking. Alexander immediately looked up.

"We need to talk."

He leaned back in his chair.

"About the project?"

"That too."

"What happened?"

Helena closed the door behind her.

"I don't know what's been happening with you over the last few weeks, but your behavior has changed."

"It hasn't."

"It has."

"Helena..."

"You started questioning things you never questioned before, interrupting meetings for reasons that don't seem related to the project, and today you decided I should return to the office in the middle of a visit without explaining why."

Alexander stood.

"I had other commitments."

"Then you could have said that."

"I said I needed to go back."

"That's not the same thing."

He walked to the window.

"You're reading too much into it."

"Maybe."

Helena took a deep breath.

"But I don't think I'm imagining it."

Alexander remained with his back to her.

"What do you want me to say?"

She hesitated.

"The truth."

He turned around.

For several seconds, the two of them simply looked at each other.

Alexander wanted to say that he was tired. That his father was sick. That the company demanded more from him than he had ever imagined. That there were days when he woke up without knowing whether he would receive bad news before lunch. He wanted to say that everything felt out of place and that, amid all of it, Helena's presence had become one of the few things that still worked the way it used to.

But he did not.

Instead, he asked:

"Do you like working with Daniel?"

Helena looked surprised.

"I do."

The answer was immediate.

Alexander felt the impact before he could hide it.

"He's competent," she continued. "And he's easy to work with."

"Easy?"

"Yes."

"Is that important to you?"

Helena frowned.

"It's important to anyone."

"I imagine."

"Alexander, what does that have to do with the project?"

He did not answer.

She watched him for several seconds, waiting for an explanation that never came. Alexander remained motionless by the window, his gaze lost over the city, as if finding some answer among the buildings could be easier than facing the question Helena had just asked.

"I don't know," he finally said.

Helena looked surprised.

It was probably the first time he had admitted not knowing something in front of her.

"It's all right," she replied.

Alexander turned.

"No, it isn't."

She said nothing.

He ran a hand over his face, exhausted.

"I don't know what's happening to me."

Helena softened her expression.

"You're going through a lot."

"It's not just that."

"Then what is it?"

Alexander opened his mouth, but no answer came out.

Because, in that moment, he realized that any answer would reveal more than he was prepared to offer.

Helena waited a few seconds.

When she saw that he would not say anything else, she simply nodded.

"I think you need some time."

"Maybe."

"Then I'll let you work."

She turned toward the door.

"Helena."

She stopped.

Alexander watched her for a moment.

"I'm sorry."

She frowned slightly.

"For what?"

"For my behavior today."

Helena held his gaze.

"It's okay."

"It isn't."

"It is."

She opened the door.

"Just try not to turn the project into a personal war."

A small smile appeared on his face.

"I can't promise that."

She smiled too.

"I figured."

And she left.

Alexander remained alone.

The room seemed larger after she left. The silence, which for years had been a kind of comfort, now seemed excessive. He walked slowly toward the desk but did not sit down. He stood beside it, looking at the documents he was supposed to review, although he knew he would not be able to concentrate.

He thought about Daniel.

About the way Helena smiled when she talked to him.

He thought about the irritation he had felt that afternoon, the absurd need to interrupt a perfectly normal situation, the way he had invented reasons to get her attention over the past few weeks. He thought about the questions he asked, the little provocations, the coffee he left waiting for her, the way he knew when she arrived early, when she was tired, when something had happened simply by the way she entered the room.

Then he thought about what had happened when she asked what was going on.

He had not been able to answer.

Because the answer had been in front of him for weeks.

Maybe since long before that.

Alexander closed his eyes for a moment and took a deep breath. He tried to find some rational explanation, some justification that would make it less inconvenient, less dangerous, less impossible to ignore. He found none. All he found were memories too small to be important and too numerous to be coincidence: the first time she had stood up to him without raising her voice, the way she corrected his arguments without fear, the concentration she assumed when she worked, the discreet way she smiled when something genuinely amused her. He also remembered the afternoon when she had learned about his father and had not tried to ask questions or offer advice he had not requested. She had simply stayed there, respecting the silence.

That was when Alexander finally stopped looking for an explanation that did not exist.

He liked her.

It was not simply curiosity, admiration, or the pleasure of finding someone who was not intimidated by him. It was not merely the attraction he had been trying to ignore since their first encounters. It was something deeper, more inconvenient, and much harder to control.

He was in love with Helena.

The realization brought no relief.

It brought silence.

Alexander opened his eyes and looked at the door through which she had just left. For the first time, he understood that the real problem was not Daniel, nor the project, nor the distance he had been trying to maintain.

It was Helena.

And the fact that, after weeks of trying to convince her—and himself—that she was merely part of his routine, he could no longer imagine his own routine without her.

chapters.title: What We Don't Say
chapters.content:
In the weeks that followed that conversation, something changed between Helena and Alexander, although neither of them had made any conscious effort to define what it was. After admitting to himself that he was in love with her, Alexander became even more careful with every gesture, as if the very awareness of that feeling had transformed everything around them into dangerous territory. He remained present at meetings, continued to be demanding about the project, and maintained the same controlled demeanor in front of the team, but he began choosing more carefully the moments when he sought Helena out, avoiding unnecessary questions and reducing the small provocations that had become so frequent. Helena noticed the change but did not know how to interpret it. Part of her believed that Alexander had finally understood the boundaries she had tried to establish; another part, much harder to silence, missed the attention that had once irritated her. Daniel continued working directly with her and, naturally, the project carried on, but his presence no longer provoked the same visible reactions in Alexander as before. The problem was not that he had stopped feeling jealous. It was that he had understood that any closeness between Helena and someone else could become irrelevant in the face of a much greater truth, a truth he still did not know how to face.

It was on a Thursday afternoon that the invitation came.

Helena was reviewing a presentation in the meeting room when Alexander appeared at the door. He did not enter immediately. He stood there for a few seconds, watching her in silence until she noticed his presence and looked up from her laptop.

"Do you need something?"

"Yes."

She partially closed the computer.

"What happened?"

"Nothing with the project."

The answer made Helena raise an eyebrow.

"Then it must be important, considering you came personally to interrupt my work."

A small smile appeared on his face.

"It's an invitation."

"An invitation?"

"To an event tomorrow night."

Helena watched him carefully.

"A company event?"

"Partly."

"That's not very enlightening."

Alexander entered the room and closed the door behind him.

"It's a reception organized by the family foundation. Some investors will be there, along with board members, longtime partners, and a few important people connected to the project."

Helena waited.

"And?"

"I want you to go."

She was silent for a moment.

"Why?"

Alexander approached the table but did not sit down.

"Because some of the people who will be there need to meet you. The project is entering a phase where institutional relationships will begin to carry the same weight as the technical work."

"Is that a professional justification?"

"It is."

Helena narrowed her eyes.

"You took a while to answer."

"Because I'm trying to decide whether I should be completely honest."

"And should you?"

Alexander held her gaze.

"Probably not."

She almost smiled.

"That wasn't very convincing."

"I also want you to go because I would rather have you by my side."

The sentence hung between them for several seconds.

Helena had not expected it.

Alexander seemed to realize that he had said more than he intended, but he did not take it back.

"By your side as part of the team," he added.

"Of course."

She looked away toward the laptop, trying to recover the natural rhythm of the conversation.

"What kind of event is it?"

"Formal."

"How formal?"

"Formal enough to make you regret asking."

Helena laughed.

"That doesn't help."

"It'll be at a hotel downtown. Dinner, music, brief speeches. Nothing very different from other events like this."

"All right," she finally said. "I'll go."

Alexander nodded.

"Thank you."

"Don't thank me yet. I might regret it."

"You can leave before dinner."

"Tempting."

He smiled.

"Eight o'clock."

"All right."

Alexander walked toward the door but stopped before leaving.

"Helena."

"Yes?"

"You don't need to worry about impressing anyone."

She frowned slightly.

"I wasn't worried."

"I know."

And he left.

Helena remained staring at the closed door for a few seconds before returning to her laptop. She tried to resume the presentation but realized she had read the same paragraph three times without absorbing a word. She did not know why the invitation had affected her so much. Alexander had already demonstrated confidence in her work many times. It was perfectly reasonable that he would want to introduce her to people involved in the project. It was a professional decision.

Still, something about that evening felt different.

Maybe because, for the first time, Alexander had not used work as his only justification.

Maybe because she had noticed.

And maybe because a part of her wanted to find out whether it meant something.

The following night, when Helena arrived at the hotel, she immediately realized that the event would be larger than she had imagined. The main ballroom occupied almost the entire ground floor, with large windows overlooking the illuminated city, carefully arranged tables, discreet floral arrangements, and low lighting that made the room seem more intimate than it actually was. People moved in small groups, speaking in moderate tones, while waiters passed among them carrying glasses and small trays. There were businessmen, investors, institutional representatives, and people Helena recognized only from news reports and photographs, names associated with important companies and families that seemed to have belonged to that circle for generations.

She discreetly adjusted the fabric of her dress before entering. She did not want to look nervous. And she wasn't. At least that was what she kept repeating to herself.

Alexander found her a few minutes later. For a moment, he simply stood there looking at her. Helena was wearing a long, elegantly cut dress without excess, in a dark shade that emphasized her skin and left her hair loose over her shoulders. There was nothing about her that seemed designed to attract attention, and perhaps that was exactly what made it impossible not to notice her.

Alexander approached.

"You came."

Helena smiled.

"You were the one who invited me."

"I know."

"Then you don't seem very surprised."

"I'm not surprised."

She studied him for a moment.

"You're different."

"How?"

"Quieter."

"I'm thinking."

"Is that usually dangerous?"

He smiled.

"Sometimes."

Before Helena could answer, an elegant woman approached them. Alexander introduced them, and over the next few minutes Helena was introduced to several people. What surprised her most was the way Alexander spoke about her work. He did not introduce her merely as the consultant hired for the project. He spoke about her analyses, her involvement in decisions, and the importance of some of the proposals she had presented. At one point, one of the investors commented on the team's experience.

"Was Alexander the one who structured this part?" he asked.

Alexander looked at Helena.

"Some of the decisions, yes. But most of the strategic analysis came from her."

Helena felt a subtle warmth rise to her face.

"The work was done as a team."

"You don't have to be modest," he said.

She looked at him.

"I'm not being modest. I'm being precise."

The man laughed.

"Now I understand why Alexander likes working with you."

Alexander did not answer.

He simply looked at Helena.

She looked away.

The rest of the evening passed in a succession of conversations, introductions, and small moments in which Alexander always seemed to know where she was. Whenever someone approached her, he remained nearby. Whenever she needed some information, he appeared before she had to look for him. When he noticed that she had been standing alone near one of the windows for a few minutes, he approached with a glass of water.

"Are you all right?"

"I am."

"Tired?"

"A little."

"Do you want to leave?"

Helena looked at him.

"Not yet."

"Are you sure?"

"Alexander, I know how to say when I want to leave."

He smiled.

"I know."

"Then stop asking."

"I'll try."

She raised her glass.

"Are you succeeding?"

"Not very well."

Helena laughed.

It was a low, spontaneous laugh, and Alexander looked at her for a moment longer than he should have.

"What?" she asked.

"Nothing."

"You're looking at me."

"I am."

The direct answer caught her by surprise.

"Why?"

Alexander moved a little closer.

"Because I like looking at you."

Helena's heart beat faster.

She could have said something. She could have made a joke, changed the subject, or reminded him that they were at an event full of people. But she did none of those things. She simply stood there, looking at Alexander, while the sound of conversations and music seemed to gradually fade away.

He was the first to look away.

"Let's go."

"Where?"

"Somewhere quieter."

Helena hesitated for only a few seconds before following him.

Alexander led her down a side corridor to a small private balcony, away from the main ballroom. The door closed behind them, almost completely muffling the sound of the event. The city stretched out before them, full of lights and movement, while the night breeze made Helena cross her arms.

"Better?" he asked.

"Much."

Alexander stood beside her, leaning against the railing.

For a while, neither of them spoke.

It was not an uncomfortable silence. It was different. There was something about that space away from everyone else that made words seem less necessary. Helena looked at the city, trying to organize her thoughts. Since she had arrived, she had noticed a change in Alexander, something more vulnerable beneath the controlled posture he wore in front of others. Maybe it was the setting. Maybe it was the absence of the responsibilities that normally surrounded them. Maybe it was simply the fact that they were alone.

"You don't usually bring people to this kind of event?" she asked.

"No."

"Then why did you bring me?"

Alexander turned his face toward her.

"I already answered."

"You didn't answer completely."

"Maybe I don't know how to answer."

Helena watched him.

"That's rare."

"Very."

"You seem uncomfortable."

"I am."

She smiled faintly.

"That's rare too."

Alexander gave a small laugh.

"You're enjoying this."

"A little."

He moved closer.

"Helena..."

She looked up.

"Yes?"

Alexander hesitated. For the first time since she had met him, he seemed not to know exactly what to do. There was no confidence in his expression, only conflict.

"I should say something."

"What?"

"That this isn't a good idea."

Helena felt her heart race.

"And is that what you think?"

Alexander remained silent.

"No."

The word came out quietly.

Helena did not step away.

He moved one step closer.

"Then what is it?"

Alexander looked at her as though he were trying to memorize that moment and, at the same time, convince her to forget it. There were so many things he wanted to say that none seemed sufficient. He wanted to tell her about the weeks he had spent trying to keep his distance, about the way she had become part of his thoughts, about his fear of letting it move forward while his own life remained surrounded by problems he could not share. He wanted to tell her the truth about his father, about the decisions he would have to make, about the people who were already beginning to watch his every move within the family and the company. But he could not. Not yet.

So he did the one thing he had been trying to avoid ever since he realized what he felt.

He kissed Helena.

The first contact was brief, almost hesitant, as though there were still one last opportunity to pull away. Helena remained still for a moment, too surprised to react, until she closed her eyes and allowed the kiss to deepen. Alexander's hand gently touched her face while his other remained at his side, as though he were still fighting the urge to pull her closer. There was no hurry. No arrogance. None of the certainty that usually accompanied that man. There was only a vulnerability Helena had never seen in him.

When they pulled apart, neither spoke immediately.

Helena opened her eyes.

Alexander was still close.

"Alexander..."

He closed his eyes for a second.

"I know."

"What was that?"

He looked at her.

The answer he wanted to give was simple.

Because I love you.

But he could not say it.

"I don't know," he replied.

Helena frowned slightly.

"That doesn't sound like a very honest answer."

"It's the only one I can give right now."

She remained silent.

Alexander lightly touched her face again, but withdrew his hand before the gesture could linger.

"We need to go back."

Helena felt a small wave of frustration.

"Of course."

They returned to the ballroom a few minutes later.

Neither mentioned the kiss.

But both of them were thinking about it.

That night, Alexander drove Helena home.

Before she got out of the car, he called her.

"Helena."

She turned.

"Yes?"

He remained silent for several seconds.

"Good night."

She waited for something more.

Nothing came.

"Good night, Alexander."

She got out of the car and entered the building.

Alexander remained parked for a few minutes, watching the lights of her apartment come on upstairs. Only then did he start the engine again.

The kiss had been a mistake, not because it had been unwanted. That was precisely the problem; it had been everything he wanted. And in that moment, Alexander understood that he would have to do something much harder than keeping his distance. He would have to make her believe that the night had meant nothing.

The next morning, Helena arrived at the office a few minutes before her usual time. She had spent much of the night trying to understand what had happened and, against her better judgment, had expected some change in the way Alexander would treat her. She did not need a declaration. She did not expect promises. She only wanted some acknowledgment that the moment had been real.

When she entered the meeting room, she found Alexander sitting at the table, reading documents. He looked up.

"Good morning."

Helena stopped for a moment.

"Good morning."

"Is the merchants' report ready?"

She stared at him.

"Yes."

"Good. We can review it before the afternoon meeting."

She left her bag on the chair.

"Of course."

Alexander returned to his documents.

It was as though nothing had happened.

Helena remained standing for a few seconds before sitting down. She opened her laptop and began searching for the report, trying to ignore the discomfort slowly growing inside her. Maybe she had expected too much. Maybe the kiss had simply been a moment of weakness for him. Maybe he regretted it. Still, the indifference felt cruel.

"Are you all right?" Alexander asked.

She looked up.

"I am."

"Good."

And he returned to work.

That one word was enough.

Helena took a deep breath, opened the first document, and spent the entire morning treating Alexander exactly as she would any other client. There was no argument. No confrontation. She did not ask why he had kissed her, nor why that morning he seemed determined to pretend it had never happened. She simply became more distant.

Alexander noticed. Every silence from her seemed like a consequence he had anticipated and, despite that, could not bear.

When Helena left the room at the end of the meeting, he remained staring at the closed door.

She had done nothing wrong.

He was the one who had chosen to kiss her.

And now he was forcing them both to pay the price for that choice.

That afternoon, Helena began avoiding moments alone with him. Whenever she could, she included Daniel or another member of the team in their conversations. She replied to Alexander's messages only with information related to the project. If she had once stayed a few minutes after meetings to discuss details, now she gathered the documents as soon as they ended and left.

Alexander did not try to stop her. That was exactly what he had decided to do. Give her space. Create distance. Protect Helena.

The problem was that she did not know from what.

She did not know that, that same night, while she was distancing herself from him, Alexander had received a call that would change everything.

The phone rang shortly after ten.

He was alone in the office, with the illuminated city behind the windows, when he saw the number on the screen. He answered immediately.

"Yes?"

The voice on the other end was low.

"We need to talk."

Alexander closed his eyes.

"About my father?"

"About him too."

"Then tell me."

There was a brief silence.

"They found out who is behind the information that was leaked."

Alexander went still.

"Who?"

The answer came with information he had feared for weeks.

The name made his stomach tighten.

"Are you sure?"

"Absolutely."

Alexander walked to the window.

"And Helena?"

"They don't know she's involved yet."

He tightened his grip on the phone.

"She's not involved."

"Alexander..."

"I said she's not involved."

"Maybe not yet."

The silence that followed seemed heavier than any argument.

Alexander looked out at the city.

He thought about the kiss.

He thought about Helena's smile on the balcony.

He thought about the way she had trusted him.

And he realized that the secret of that night was much bigger than the kiss he was now pretending had never happened.

If someone discovered what was really happening within the Blackwood family, Helena could become a target simply because she was close to him.

And he would not allow that.

Even if, to protect her, he had to make her believe that he should never have allowed that kiss to happen.

Alexander ended the call and remained alone by the window.

For the first time, he understood that perhaps the greatest risk was not losing Helena.

It was keeping her close enough for her to discover the truth.

And while he tried to decide how far he was willing to go to keep her safe, Helena, on the other side of the city, was making a much simpler decision.

She would distance herself.

Not because she had stopped feeling something.

But because she was not willing to accept being treated as though what had happened between them had meant absolutely nothing.

Neither of them knew that night that they were making decisions based on the same thing.

A secret.

And when it finally came to light, neither of them would be able to see that night in the same way again.

chapters.title: The Blackwood Secret
chapters.content:
In the days that followed the event, Helena did everything she could to turn her routine into a predictable sequence of tasks, meetings, and deadlines. She arrived early, worked as long as necessary, participated in meetings with the same attention as always, and avoided being alone with Alexander for longer than strictly necessary. There was no conversation about the kiss. No explanation. Alexander seemed determined to act as though that night had never happened, and Helena, after spending several days trying to find some justification for it, finally decided that she would no longer look for answers where none were clearly being offered. It was a rational, mature decision and, at least in theory, a simple one. In practice, however, all it took was Alexander walking into a room for every certainty she had carefully constructed that morning to begin losing its strength. The problem was not only remembering the kiss. It was remembering the way he had looked at her beforehand, the hesitation she had never seen in him, the careful touch on her face, and that brief vulnerability that contrasted so sharply with the man who usually controlled every detail around him. Helena could not believe that it had been nothing more than a mistake. And it was precisely because she believed it had not been that his attitude hurt even more.

Alexander, for his part, had spent those same mornings doing exactly the opposite of what he wanted. He kept his distance, avoided any situation that might leave them alone, and limited their conversations to the project, even when every fiber of his body seemed to want to break through the barrier he himself had created. He knew Helena was hurt. He could see it in the way she avoided his eyes, in the sudden formality of her messages, and in how quickly she ended every conversation. But he could not fix it without putting something much greater at risk. The phone call that night continued to echo in his mind, as did the name he had heard on the other end of the line. For weeks, Alexander had suspected that someone within the family's closest circle was providing confidential information about the company, but until then it had seemed like nothing more than a financial threat. Now he knew it was something more complex. Documents had disappeared, internal movements had been monitored, and board decisions were reaching outsiders before they had even been formalized. The worst part was not discovering that there was a betrayal. It was realizing that it came from someone who knew the Blackwoods intimately.

That Monday, Alexander arrived at the office before six in the morning.

The building was still almost empty. The automatic hallway lights had just come on when he crossed the lobby and entered the private elevator. There were no employees, meetings, or ringing phones. Only the silence that, for years, had been enough to allow him to think.

That morning, however, the silence did not help.

As soon as he entered his office, he opened the safe behind one of the bookshelves and removed a black folder. He placed it on the desk and stared at it for a few seconds before opening it. Inside were copies of contracts, financial records, medical reports, and internal Blackwood Holdings documents. Some were marked with small handwritten notes. Others contained dates that repeated throughout the past few months.

Alexander picked up one of the reports.

His father's name appeared at the top.

He read the information again, although he already knew it by heart.

Richard Blackwood's health had deteriorated considerably. The treatment was no longer producing the expected results, and the doctors had recommended a change in protocol that would require a decision his father had been postponing for weeks. At the same time, the company's board was pressuring Alexander to officially assume a position that had remained in his father's hands until then. Succession was being discussed in private meetings, and Alexander knew that some members of the family would not easily accept the change.

His father had spent decades building that empire.

Now he was slowly disappearing inside his hospital room.

Alexander closed the folder.

The phone on his desk rang.

"Alexander."

His older brother's voice came through the other end.

"Are you at the office?"

"I am."

"We need to talk before the board meeting."

Alexander remained silent for a few seconds.

"About what?"

"You know."

"I want to hear it from you."

There was a pause.

"The information reached the press."

Alexander closed his eyes.

"What information?"

"The documents about the succession."

He stood up.

"That should never have left here."

"I know."

"Who had access?"

"Very few people."

"Then find out which one of them talked."

"It's not that simple."

Alexander walked to the window.

"For me, it is."

"You're making this personal."

"It is personal."

"Not necessarily."

Alexander laughed without humor.

"Someone is trying to weaken our position before our father transfers power. If that isn't personal, I don't know what is."

His brother remained silent on the other end.

"There's one more thing," he said after a few seconds.

Alexander went still.

"What?"

"They're asking about the revitalization project."

Alexander's hand tightened around the phone.

"Who?"

"Some people on the board."

"Why?"

"Because the project involves properties that could increase significantly in value after approval. If privileged information is circulating, some people could make a great deal of money."

Alexander looked at the folder lying open on the desk.

Then he thought of Helena.

She had access to the project's data.

She had contact with merchants, investors, and members of the team.

And, most importantly, she trusted him.

"No one talks to Helena," he said.

"Alexander..."

"No one."

"She's directly involved in the project. Naturally..."

"I know exactly where she's involved."

"Then you understand the problem."

Alexander remained silent.

"If someone is trying to use the project to pressure the family, she could end up in the middle of it without realizing it."

"I know."

"Then you need to remove her."

Alexander closed his eyes.

The idea was exactly what he had been trying to avoid.

"Not yet."

"You're making this personal again."

"No."

The answer came quietly.

"I'm trying not to destroy the life of someone who has nothing to do with this family."

The call ended a few minutes later.

Alexander remained by the window.

He knew he should remove her from the project.

But he also knew that doing so without an explanation would raise questions.

And questions were exactly what he could not allow at that moment.

Shortly after eight, Helena entered the meeting room with a folder in her hands. Alexander was already there.

She stopped when she realized they were alone.

"Good morning."

"Good morning."

Helena walked to the table.

"Is Daniel coming?"

"I asked him to attend another meeting."

She looked at Alexander.

"Another meeting?"

"With the communications team."

"All right."

She sat down and opened the folder.

The silence that settled between them was different from the silences before. Helena had already learned to live with the tension between them, but now there was something colder, almost too careful.

"The data from the last survey is here," she said.

Alexander nodded.

"I saw it."

"Then we can begin."

He studied her face for a few seconds.

"Helena."

She looked up.

"Yes?"

"About the event..."

Her chest tightened.

Finally.

"Yes?"

Alexander hesitated.

"It shouldn't have happened."

Her face remained still, but something inside her seemed to sink.

"I understand."

Alexander noticed the change in her expression.

"Helena..."

"You don't need to explain."

"I do."

"No, Alexander. You don't."

She stood.

"I understand."

"I don't think you do."

She gave a small laugh, but there was no humor in it.

"I think I understand perfectly. You invited me to an event, kissed me when we were alone, and the next day decided that it shouldn't have happened. There's not much to interpret."

Alexander felt guilt pass through him.

"It wasn't that simple."

"For me, it was."

She gathered the documents.

"And maybe that's better."

"What does that mean?"

Helena tucked the folder under her arm.

"It means we can keep working."

"Helena..."

She finally looked at him.

"I'm not going to turn this into a professional problem."

"I know."

"Then you don't need to worry."

She walked toward the door.

Alexander remained still.

"I do worry."

Helena stopped for a moment but did not turn around.

"That's the problem."

And she left.

Alexander closed his eyes.

For a few seconds, he remained alone in the room.

Then he picked up the phone.

"Call Daniel."

The assistant answered from the other end.

"Now?"

"Now."

A few minutes later, Daniel entered.

"You wanted to see me?"

Alexander pointed to the chair.

"Sit down."

Daniel immediately noticed that something was different.

"Did something happen?"
