There were only the two of them, finally without pretending that what existed between them was merely a distraction or an inconvenient consequence of work. The silence between them no longer felt like a barrier, but rather a kind of safe space where Helena could simply remain without having to make a decision about what would come next.

But reality returned when Alexander's phone vibrated. He reluctantly stepped away and looked at the screen.

It was his brother.

**We need to talk. We found out who authorized the transfer to the intermediary company.**

Alexander opened the next message.

**It was someone inside the family.**

Helena noticed his expression change.

—What happened?

He showed her the screen.

She read it.

—Someone in the family.

Alexander nodded.

—That changes everything.

—Who?

—They haven't said yet.

Helena remained silent for a few seconds, absorbing the new information.

—So it's not over yet.

—No.

He looked at her.

—And I think we're closer to the truth now than we've been in years.

Helena nodded slowly.

—Then let's find out.

Alexander held her gaze.

—Together?

She did not answer immediately. She simply remained there before him, still processing everything that had happened in that room, everything he had told her and, above all, everything that was beginning to exist between them. After a few seconds, she nodded.

—Together.

The word was quiet, but it was enough. At the end of the afternoon, the two of them were still in the office when Helena looked at the old photograph again.

—Alexander.

—What is it?

She pointed to the image.

—The message said to ask who was driving.

—Yes.

—But it didn't ask who caused the accident.

Alexander became serious.

—No.

—Maybe because the person who sent it knows it wasn't you.

He thought for a few seconds.

—Or because they want us to find out who really did it.

Helena ran her fingers along the edge of the photograph.

—Then that's the next question.

Alexander nodded.

—And I think I already know where to look.

—Where?

He looked at the folder that was still open on the desk.

—In the documents my father hid.

Helena did not answer. She simply continued looking at the papers, trying to understand how many other things might be hidden among those pages.

Then Alexander's phone vibrated again. This time, there was no text. Only a photograph.

He opened the image.

It was an old road, probably the same stretch where the accident had happened. The photograph appeared to have been taken from a distance, perhaps around the same time as the accident. The wrecked car was partially visible beside the road and, in the corner of the image, almost hidden in the shadow of a tree, there was a second person.

Alexander enlarged the photograph. Helena moved closer to see better. The two of them remained silent.

Because that man was not in the photograph from the reception. He did not appear in any of the documents they had found. And yet Alexander recognized him immediately. Helena noticed the change in his face.

—Who is he?

Alexander took a few seconds to answer.

—Someone who was working for the Blackwood family at the time.

—And today?

He continued staring at the photograph.

—He still works for us.

Helena felt the weight of that answer.

—Do you trust him?

Alexander raised his eyes to her.

This time, he did not answer immediately.

And it was precisely that silence that made Helena understand that the next truth might be even harder than all the ones that had come before.

chapters.title: The Truth That Remained
chapters.content:
Helena remained standing before the photograph without saying anything. The man beside the car looked familiar, but the age of the image and the distance made identification difficult. Alexander continued staring at the picture with an expression she could not completely interpret. There was recognition in his eyes, but also something deeper, a kind of exhaustion that seemed to come from long before she had become part of that story. He reached out and took the photograph, holding it closer to the light.

“I know this man.”

Helena did not look away from him.

“Who is he?”

Alexander ran his thumb along the edge of the photograph.

“Thomas Reed.”

“Who?”

“He worked for Blackwood back then. Not directly for my father. He was responsible for security at some of the properties and occasionally accompanied my brother on certain operations.”

Helena felt her heart begin to race.

“And he was at the accident?”

Alexander nodded slowly.

“He was.”

“Then he saw what happened.”

“He probably saw more than he ever told me.”

Alexander turned the photograph over and examined the back.

“I don't remember that.”

“Don't remember what?”

“His presence.”

Helena frowned.

“How can you not remember someone who was standing near the car?”

Alexander remained silent for a few seconds.

“Because I was inside the car.”

The words came quietly, without dramatization. Helena felt the weight of that memory again, now that she knew it in detail. For years, Alexander had carried the accident as an unresolved part of his own life, a memory he had never been able to completely make sense of. Thomas's face, however, seemed to bring another dimension to that night.

“Could he have caused the accident?”

Alexander did not answer immediately.

“If he was there before we arrived, he could have had access to the car. But that doesn't prove anything.”

“What if he was the one who tampered with the brakes?”

“We need to find out.”

Alexander picked up his phone.

“I'll call my brother.”

“No.”

He raised his eyes.

“Why?”

“Because if someone inside the family authorized the transfer to the intermediary company, your brother may not know who he can trust either.”

Alexander hesitated.

“He's my brother.”

“I know.”

“I trust him.”

Helena held his gaze.

“Then find out first whether he can trust you.”

Alexander remained silent for a few seconds, then nodded. There was no irritation on his face. Only the realization that Helena was right. All this time, they had tried to separate the truth into manageable pieces, as though it were possible to investigate one part without touching the others. But now the pieces were finally coming together: the properties, the intermediary companies, Daniel's father, Victoria, the accident, Thomas Reed, and the transfer authorized by someone inside the family.

Alexander called his brother.

“Did you find out who authorized the transfer?”

The answer came from the other end.

“Yes.”

Alexander went still.

“Who?”

There was a pause.

“Thomas Reed.”

A shiver ran through Helena. Alexander closed his eyes.

“Are you sure?”

“The document has his signature. And we found records of payments to the intermediary company for almost three years.”

“Who authorized the payments?”

“At first, Richard.”

Alexander opened his eyes and looked at Helena.

“And afterward?”

The answer took a few seconds.

“Afterward, Thomas was given authorization to move the funds on behalf of the company.”

Alexander fell silent.

“That doesn't mean he created everything,” his brother continued. “But it means he had enough access to do it.”

“And the company?”

“It was controlled by someone else.”

“Who?”

“We're still confirming that.”

Alexander tightened his grip on the phone.

“I need the name.”

“Alexander...”

“I need it now.”

His brother took a deep breath.

“Harold Blackwood.”

The silence that followed seemed to fill the entire room.

Helena looked at Alexander.

He did not move.

“Who is Harold?” she asked as soon as the call ended.

Alexander took a moment to answer.

“Our uncle.”

Helena felt her stomach tighten.

“Your father's brother?”

“Yes.”

“Is he still alive?”

“He is.”

“And does he still work for the family?”

Alexander let out a slow breath.

“For years.”

The pieces began fitting together with an unsettling precision. Harold had access to the family, the businesses, and the old information. Thomas had physical access to the properties and, later, to the financial transactions. Richard had authorized the initial operations, but afterward the payments came under Thomas's control. Daniel's father had discovered something, tried to expose the scheme, and shortly afterward suffered an accident in which the brakes had been tampered with.

Helena looked at the photograph again.

“Was your uncle there that night?”

Alexander frowned.

“I don't remember seeing him.”

“But Thomas was.”

“Yes.”

“And Thomas worked for him?”

Alexander ran a hand through his hair.

“Officially, Thomas reported to security. In practice, he could receive orders from any family member with enough influence.”

Helena slowly walked toward the window.

“Then maybe your father wasn't the one who ordered the accident.”

Alexander remained silent.

“But he knew about the companies.”

“He did.”

“And he knew your uncle was involved?”

Alexander looked at her.

“Maybe.”

The word seemed insufficient.

“Alexander.”

He took a deep breath.

“My father knew money was being moved. He knew some properties had been acquired in questionable ways. But at the time, I didn't know whether he was trying to find out who was behind it or trying to protect the family.”

“And after the accident?”

“After the accident, he tried to shut the matter down.”

Helena felt the answer weigh on her.

“So he knew something was wrong.”

“Yes.”

“And he still let everything continue.”

Alexander lowered his eyes.

“That is the part of him I could never forgive.”

She moved closer.

“And you?”

“I have blame too.”

“No.”

“I lied about the folder.”

“Because you were afraid.”

“I should have told someone.”

“You were young.”

Alexander let out a small, humorless laugh.

“Not that young.”

Helena stopped in front of him.

“You were his son, you were inside a car that crashed, and you had just heard a seriously injured man tell you not to trust your father. There was no way you could have understood all of that.”

Alexander held her gaze.

“Maybe not.”

“And you spent years trying to solve something on your own that you were never supposed to carry alone.”

He remained silent.

For a few moments, neither of them spoke. The tension between them had changed. For the first time, it was no longer the tension of two people trying to determine whether they could trust each other. It was the silence of two people finally beginning to understand the weight the other had been carrying.

Helena's phone vibrated, and she looked at the screen. It was a message from Daniel.

“I need to talk to you. I found something about my father.”

Helena showed the message to Alexander.

“Let's go.”

“Are you sure?”

“If we're trying to find the truth, we can't stop now.”

Daniel was waiting for them in a private room in the building. He stood beside a table covered with old documents, photographs, and several sheets that appeared to have come from personal archives.

When Helena entered, he looked up.

“I found this after our conversation.”

Alexander stepped closer.

“What is it?”

Daniel picked up a photograph.

“My father.”

In the image, a younger man stood in front of an old building. Richard Blackwood and Harold stood beside him.

Alexander took the photograph.

“Where did you find it?”

“In a box my mother kept for years.”

Helena moved closer.

“What else was in there?”

Daniel opened a folder.

“Letters.”

He handed one to Alexander, who read it silently before passing it to Helena. The letter was from Daniel's father to Richard.

The text was not long, but it made it clear that he had discovered certain properties were being purchased by companies that concealed the true beneficiaries. He mentioned Harold and Thomas and wrote that he had found evidence that inside information was being used to anticipate the appreciation of the properties.

At the end was a sentence that made Alexander remain still for several seconds.

“If anything happens to me, don't look for who signed the documents. Look for who had access before they were signed.”

Helena raised her eyes.

“That explains the folder.”

Alexander nodded.

“And it explains why he wanted to give me the documents.”

Daniel watched the two of them.

“My father knew he was in danger?”

“Yes,” Alexander said.

Daniel ran a hand over his face.

“And I never knew.”

“You were young,” Helena said.

“Even so.”

Alexander placed the letter on the table.

“There is something else.”

He told Daniel about Thomas, the transfer to the intermediary company, and the photograph from the accident.

Daniel fell silent.

“So it was him?”

Alexander took a deep breath.

“We still don't know if he was the one who tampered with the brakes. But we know he was at the scene and that, years later, he received money from the company used to conceal the assets.”

Daniel closed his eyes.

“My father was right.”

“He was,” Alexander replied.

For a few seconds, no one spoke.

Then Daniel opened another folder.

“There is more.”

He pulled out an old sheet of paper.

“This was with the letters.”

Alexander picked up the document. It was an internal order dated two days before the accident.

Thomas Reed's name appeared at the top.

Below it was an authorization granting access to the vehicle Alexander had used that night.

Helena felt a shiver run through her body.

“The brakes.”

Alexander read it again.

At the bottom of the page was a signature.

Harold Blackwood.

This time, there was no doubt.

The mystery that had remained hidden for years finally had a face, a signature, and a sequence of events that no longer depended on assumptions. Harold had discovered that Daniel's father intended to hand the documents over to the authorities and feared the investigation would reach the family's interests. Thomas, working under his orders, gained access to Alexander's car. The accident had been planned to look like a mechanical failure. Daniel Morgan had been included in the documents years later only because his name had been used as the representative of a company connected to his father, without his knowing participation. Richard knew there was corruption within the family, but instead of reporting his own brother, he tried to contain the problem and protect the Blackwood name. His silence had protected the family for a time, but it had also allowed the structure to continue existing.

Alexander closed his eyes.

“My father knew.”

Helena gently touched his arm.

“He knew part of it.”

“Enough to have done something.”

“Maybe he tried.”

“Not enough.”

His voice was low.

Helena gently squeezed his arm.

“You can't change what he did.”

Alexander looked at her.

“No.”

“But you can decide what to do now.”

He remained silent.

Daniel looked at the two of them and, for the first time since Helena had met him, seemed to understand that this story was not only about money or companies. It was about people who had spent years trying to survive the consequences of decisions made by others.

“What are you going to do?” he asked.

Alexander looked at the documents.

“Hand everything over to the lawyers and the authorities.”

Daniel nodded.

“And my father?”

Alexander picked up the letter.

“His name will be removed from any accusation created using these documents.”

Daniel took a deep breath.

“Thank you.”

“I am sorry for what happened to him.”

Daniel lowered his eyes.

“So am I.”

The silence that followed was not uncomfortable. For the first time, it felt final.

Helena looked at the documents scattered across the table and realized that no essential piece was missing anymore. The past would continue to exist, and perhaps it would never be possible to completely repair everything that had happened, but the truth no longer depended on anonymous messages, hidden photographs, or incomplete versions. Harold would be held accountable for what he had done. Thomas would answer for his involvement. The financial operations could be investigated. Richard would have to face the consequences of having remained silent. And Daniel would finally know that his father had tried to stop that story from continuing.

The mystery that had invaded Helena's life for weeks ended there, not because every wound could be erased, but because there was finally a complete truth in place of suspicion.

Later, when they left the building, Helena noticed that Alexander was walking beside her in silence.

There was no phone ringing.

No unknown message.

No photograph arriving from a number she did not know.

No secret meeting waiting for them.

For the first time in a long while, silence did not mean that someone was hiding something.

Alexander stopped beside the car.

“Helena.”

She turned.

“Yes?”

He watched her for several seconds before speaking.

“I am sorry.”

“For what?”

“For deciding on my own what you should know. For trying to protect you without realizing that I was making you feel excluded. And for allowing fear to make my decisions for me.”

Helena remained standing before him.

“You were afraid of losing me.”

Alexander did not deny it.

“I was.”

“And you thought pushing me away would be safer.”

“I did.”

She took a deep breath.

“Did it work?”

He almost smiled.

“No.”

Helena smiled too, but her smile slowly faded when she became aware of how close they were.

“It didn't work because you can't decide on your own what I feel.”

“I know.”

“And because you can't protect me from everything.”

“I know.”

“And because I don't want you to try.”

Alexander took a step closer.

“What do you want?”

Helena felt her heart race.

For weeks, that question would have been impossible to answer. There had been too many secrets between them, too much fear, too many things left unsaid. Now, for the first time, none of those barriers remained hidden between them. All that was left was what they had tried to ignore from the very beginning.

She raised her eyes.

“I want you to stop running away.”

Alexander went still.

“From what?”

Helena smiled faintly.

“You know.”

He moved closer.

“Maybe I'm tired of running.”

“Then don't run.”

Alexander raised his hand to her face, touching her skin with a gentleness that contrasted with all the tension of the past few weeks.

“Helena...”

She did not answer.

Neither did he say anything else.

He simply kissed her.

This time, there was no hurry, fear, or guilt hidden in the gesture. The kiss did not need to interrupt an argument or serve as a promise for the future. It was simply what they both wanted in that moment, after weeks in which they had allowed secrets, responsibilities, and fears to occupy the space that belonged to them.

When they pulled apart, they remained close.

Helena rested her forehead against his.

“You still have a lot to learn.”

Alexander smiled.

“I imagined as much.”

“Especially about trust.”

“I can learn.”

“You'll have to.”

“With you?”

Helena looked at him.

“If you can keep up.”

His smile widened.

“I think I can.”

She shook her head, amused, and finally stepped back a little.

“Don't get too confident.”

“I'm trying.”

“It doesn't look like it.”

Alexander laughed softly.

It was the first time Helena had heard that laugh without any tension behind it.

And in that moment, she realized that perhaps this was exactly what had been missing between them from the beginning: not an answer to the past, nor a perfect explanation for everything that had happened, but the possibility of looking at each other without having to search for a hidden threat.

The past would continue to exist. The consequences would still have to be faced, the documents would be handed over, those responsible would answer for what they had done, and Richard would have his own choices to explain. But that no longer belonged only to Helena and Alexander. The story that had threatened to separate them had finally stopped being a secret between them.

Alexander opened the car door.

“Can I take you home?”

Helena got in, but before closing the door, she looked at him.

“You can.”

He walked around the car and got into the driver's seat.

For several minutes, neither of them spoke. The city continued its usual rhythm around them, the old buildings remained illuminated by the late afternoon light, and the streets that had seemed full of shadows for weeks now looked like nothing more than streets. Helena looked out the window and felt a sense of peace she had not experienced in a long time.

Alexander extended his hand across the center console.

This time, there was no secret in the gesture.

Helena looked at his hand for a moment before intertwining her fingers with his.

And neither of them needed to say anything else.

chapters.title: The Last Answers
chapters.content:
The following morning, Helena woke with the strange feeling that, after so many weeks of trying to piece together fragments that seemed to belong to different stories, she could finally see the whole picture. The accident, the missing documents, the intermediary companies, Harold, Thomas Reed, the families’ involvement in the past, and Daniel’s name being used without his knowledge. All of it had stopped being a succession of disconnected questions. But there was still one thing that bothered her. A question that had nothing to do with the accident, the documents, or the succession. A much more personal question.

Who had taken the photographs?

Helena was sitting across from Alexander when she finally decided to ask about it.

“I need to know something.”

Alexander looked up.

“What?”

“The photographs.”

He remained silent for a few seconds.

There was no surprise on his face. Only that same weight Helena had learned to recognize whenever an unpleasant memory returned to the surface.

“I knew you would ask.”

“You received more than one?”

Alexander nodded.

“Yes.”

“How many?”

“Several.”

Helena felt a discomfort move through her body.

“And they were all of me?”

“All of them.”

“Taken from where?”

“Different places. Leaving the office, entering your building, some during the project. One of them was taken near a restaurant where you were with Daniel.”

She stared at him.

“And you never knew who was doing it?”

“No.”

The answer came without hesitation.

“I tried to find out. I increased security, asked them to check the cameras near the places where you appeared, and tried to trace any information that could lead to the source of the images. But whoever was doing it knew how to avoid leaving an obvious trail.”

“Why were they sending the photographs to you?”

Alexander looked away.

“So I would know they were close to you.”

“That doesn’t explain everything.”

“No.”

He ran a hand over his face.

“It was a form of pressure.”

Helena felt the understanding slowly take shape.

“Against you.”

“Yes.”

“They wanted you to know they could reach me.”

Alexander nodded.

“And that I wouldn’t be able to keep you out of it.”

She looked at him for several seconds.

“Did you recognize any place? Anyone?”

“Not in the photographs.”

“Then how do we find out?”

Alexander picked up the phone from the table and opened a folder of documents.

“That was exactly what changed yesterday.”

He showed her a series of records.

“My brother managed to cross-reference some of the old financial documents with the access records we found after the lawyers began reviewing the material.”

Helena moved closer.

“Thomas Reed.”

Alexander nodded.

“Thomas Reed.”

The name remained between them.

Helena already knew him from the documents that had appeared during the investigation. She knew he had had access to properties, vehicles, and operations connected to the family’s old structure. But now the piece seemed to fit differently.

“He had enough access to do this.”

“Yes.”

“And he was connected to Harold.”

“He was.”

Helena looked back at the documents.

“So it was him.”

Alexander took a deep breath.

“It was him.”

The answer should have brought relief. Instead, Helena felt a shiver.

For weeks, the idea of someone watching her movements had remained a faceless threat. Now it had a name.

Thomas Reed.

A man who did not need to invent a way to reach her. He already had access to properties, vehicles, records, and people within the family’s old structure. He knew how to move around without attracting attention. He knew how to obtain information. And, most importantly, he had a reason.

“Why would Thomas do this?”

“Because Harold needed to keep me under pressure.”

“After you started investigating the past.”

“Yes.”

Alexander closed the folder.

“When I realized there was something wrong with the documents, I started asking questions I wasn’t supposed to ask. After I discovered some of the movements connected to the accident, the photographs began appearing more frequently.”

Helena watched him.

“And you thought that if you pushed me away, they would lose interest.”

Alexander held her gaze.

“I thought it would reduce the risk.”

She did not answer.

There was no need to return to that argument. He had already explained why he had distanced himself after the reception and the kiss. Helena knew that decision had come from fear and from his attempt to protect her. The problem now was something else.

She moved closer to the table.

“You should have told me about the photographs.”

“I know.”

“Even if it was going to scare me.”

“I know.”

“Because I was living normally while someone was recording my movements.”

Alexander lowered his eyes.

“I know.”

The sincerity of his answer softened some of her irritation.

Helena took a deep breath.

“Then why did you keep it from me?”

“Because I was trying to solve everything before putting one more thing on your shoulders.”

She stared at him.

“Alexander, you need to stop deciding on your own what I can handle.”

He remained silent.

“I don’t want you to protect me by keeping me in the dark.”

Alexander nodded slowly.

“I understand.”

“Do you really?”

“This time, yes.”

Helena looked at him for a few seconds.

“And your messages? Who was sending them to you?”

“Victoria.”

Alexander took a deep breath.

“You think it was her?”

“I’m certain.”

Alexander frowned.

“How?”

“Because she told me.”

The silence that followed was different.

Alexander leaned back in his chair.

“She spoke to you?”

“Yes.”

“When?”

Helena told him about the meeting, the documents, and the way Victoria had guided the conversation from the beginning. She also told him that Victoria had confirmed she was the person behind the anonymous messages.

Alexander listened without interrupting.

“So it was her.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because she wanted me to discover the truth.”

Alexander became thoughtful.

“Victoria always believed my father should have exposed what was happening back then. When she realized no one was going to do it, she decided to find another way to put the information in front of someone who could not simply ignore it.”

“And that person was me.”

“You were close to me. You had access to the project. And, most importantly, you weren’t part of that old story.”

Helena nodded.

“She also wanted you to talk.”

Alexander looked away.

“I imagined that.”

“The messages weren’t only for me.”

“No.”

“They were meant to pressure you.”

Alexander remained silent for a few seconds.

“Victoria knew I was trying to keep you out of this. Maybe she realized that if she continued speaking only to me, I would find another way to postpone everything again.”

Helena gave a small smile.

“She probably realized that before you did.”

Alexander smiled for the first time.

“Possibly.”

The silence between them became lighter.

Helena returned to the two questions.

“So we have two different people.”

“Yes.”

“Victoria sent the messages.”

“Yes.”

“And Thomas took the photographs.”

Alexander nodded.

“Thomas worked for Harold.”

“And Victoria was trying to reveal what Harold and Thomas were hiding.”

“Exactly.”

Helena leaned back in her chair.

Finally.

Two different questions.

Two different answers.

For so long, she had imagined that all those things came from the same person, as though there had been a single hand controlling every detail. Now she understood that the situation was more complicated. Victoria had chosen to act in order to expose the truth. Thomas had acted to hide it and maintain Harold’s control.

“One was trying to open the door,” Helena said.

“The other was trying to keep it closed.”

“I want to find Victoria,” Helena said.

Alexander nodded.

“We can do that.”

“Not to ask about the documents.”

“I know.”

“I want to thank her.”

Alexander smiled faintly.

“I don’t think she expects thanks.”

“Even so.”

He stood.

“Then let’s go.”

Victoria received them that same afternoon in a small rented office downtown, far from the Blackwood building. There were no documents scattered across the table this time. No old folders. No photographs.

Only three chairs and an open window facing the street.

Victoria looked at Helena first.

“You found out.”

“I did.”

Then she looked at Alexander.

“And you finally told her everything.”

Alexander let out a sigh.

“Not exactly everything.”

Victoria raised an eyebrow.

“Alexander.”

“I’m learning.”

Helena smiled.

Victoria seemed satisfied with the answer.

“Then perhaps my messages served some purpose after all.”

Helena sat down.

“They did.”

“I’m sorry for the way I did it.”

“You could have simply talked to me.”

Victoria gave a small smile.

“Would you have believed me?”

Helena thought for a moment.

“Probably not.”

“That’s what I thought.”

Alexander sat beside Helena.

“Did you know about the photographs?”

Victoria became serious.

“I did.”

Helena watched her.

“Did you take any of them?”

“No.”

The answer came immediately.

“Then you knew who was doing it?”

Victoria nodded.

“I found out later.”

“Thomas?”

“Thomas Reed.”

Helena felt her body tense.

“How did you find out?”

“Because some of the information he used to find you appeared in the same records I had discovered years ago. Schedules, access records, vehicle movements. At first, I couldn’t prove it was him. Later, I could.”

Alexander remained still.

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

Victoria looked directly at him.

“Because you weren’t ready to hear it.”

“I was receiving the photographs.”

“Exactly.”

Alexander frowned.

Victoria continued:

“You already knew someone was watching Helena. What you didn’t know was why. If I had simply sent you Thomas’s name, you would have gone after him before understanding who was above him.”

Helena understood the logic.

“Harold.”

“Harold.”

Victoria folded her hands on the table.

“Thomas wasn’t responsible for everything. He was someone who did the work Harold needed done.”

“And the photographs were a form of threat,” Helena said.

“More than that. They were a form of control.”

Alexander nodded slowly.

“To remind me that they could reach her.”

“Yes.”

Helena looked at Victoria.

“So you knew I was being watched and still continued sending me messages.”

Victoria did not look away.

“Because I needed you to keep asking questions.”

“Even with the risk?”

“I knew there was a risk. I didn’t know Thomas would get that close to you.”

Helena remained silent.

There was no pride in Victoria’s voice. No justification. Only a tired honesty.

“You could have told me.”

“I could have.”

“Why didn’t you?”

Victoria looked at Alexander.

“Because I wanted him to tell you.”

Helena understood.

Victoria stood and walked toward the window.

“For years, everyone decided what the others should know. Richard protected the family name. Harold protected his own interests. Thomas protected Harold. Alexander tried to protect you. And I tried to protect the documents.”

She turned around.

“In the end, no one was telling the whole truth to anyone.”

Alexander lowered his eyes.

Helena looked at him.

“That needs to end.”

He raised his face.

“It has.”

Victoria nodded.

“Now it has.”

Later, Helena and Alexander walked slowly through the streets downtown.

There was no longer any need to talk about documents.

There were no more hidden names.

There were no more anonymous messages waiting for an answer.

Helena held his hand.

Alexander looked at their intertwined fingers.

“Are you feeling calm?”

“Not completely yet.”

“Neither am I.”

She smiled.

“At least now we know why.”

Alexander gently squeezed her hand.

“I spent so much time trying to control everything that I forgot some things can’t be controlled.”

“Like what?”

He looked at her.

“You.”

Helena raised an eyebrow.

“Was that supposed to be romantic?”

Alexander smiled.

“I’m trying.”

She laughed.

“You’re getting better.”

They continued walking.

For a few minutes, neither of them spoke. The city moved around them, filled with people who had no idea how much had happened over the past few months. To Helena, that normality felt almost strange. For so long, every unknown call, every door that closed, and every change in Alexander’s behavior had seemed to carry a hidden threat.

Not anymore.

Now she knew.

Victoria had sent the messages.

Thomas had taken the photographs.

Harold had used Thomas to maintain control.

And Alexander had finally stopped hiding from her what needed to be faced.

She stopped.

Alexander stopped too.

“What is it?”

“Nothing.”

“Are you sure?”

“I am.”

She held his face between her hands and kissed him.

Alexander returned the kiss with the same intensity he had tried to hide for so long, but without the tension of the previous months. When they pulled apart, he kept his forehead against hers.

“I love you,” he said.

Helena smiled.

“I know.”

He laughed softly.

“That wasn’t the answer I was expecting.”

“What did you want me to say?”

“Maybe that you love me too.”

She watched him for a few seconds, as though she wanted to make him wait a little longer.

“I love you too.”

Alexander closed his eyes for a moment.

“Now that’s better.”

Helena ran her fingers over his face.

“But I still have one condition.”

“What?”

“No disappearing to protect me.”

“Agreed.”

“No deciding on your own what I can or cannot know.”

“Agreed.”

“And if you receive another photograph of me...”

Alexander smiled.

“I’ll tell you immediately.”

“Good.”

He kissed her again.

When they began walking once more, Helena realized that something had changed. Not because all the difficult things had disappeared, but because, for the first time, they no longer had to face them separately.

chapters.title: Where It All Begins
chapters.content:
A few weeks later, life finally began to feel like something Helena recognized. Not because everything had returned exactly to the way it had been before, but because, for the first time in a long while, she no longer had to enter a room expecting to discover something someone had hidden from her. The documents were with the lawyers, the authorities had received the necessary material, and the old financial transactions were being investigated by the people responsible for doing so. Harold no longer had the control he had maintained for so many years, and Thomas Reed had disappeared from the Blackwood family’s routine with the same quietness with which he had once moved through it. Richard continued receiving medical care, more fragile than before, but finally surrounded by people who no longer needed to protect their silences. Daniel had continued along his professional path after officially clarifying that his name had been used without his knowledge, and the relationship between him and Helena had found a simple sense of peace, without the suspicions that had hung over them for some time. But above all those changes, there was one Helena noticed every day: Alexander was different. He had not become less reserved, nor had he lost that controlled way of observing everything before acting, but he no longer closed doors when she approached. When something happened, he told her. When he needed time, he said so. When he was afraid, sometimes he even admitted it. And to Helena, that was worth more than any grand declaration.

That Friday, however, Alexander seemed particularly mysterious. Helena noticed it first thing in the morning, when he appeared at the door of her office shortly before lunchtime, wearing a dark suit without a tie and carrying only his car keys. He rested one hand against the doorframe and looked at her with an expression she knew far too well to believe his attempt to appear casual.

“Are you busy?”

Helena looked up from her computer.

“That question usually means you’re about to do something I haven’t been informed about.”

“Maybe.”

“Alexander.”

He smiled.

“Do you trust me?”

Helena narrowed her eyes.

“That question is even worse.”

He stepped into the office and approached the desk.

“I need you to leave early today.”

“Why?”

“Because I want to take you somewhere.”

“Where?”

“If I tell you, it ruins the surprise.”

Helena crossed her arms.

“You know asking me to trust you after everything that happened isn’t exactly a brilliant strategy.”

Alexander smiled sideways.

“That’s exactly why I’m asking.”

She watched him for a few seconds. There was something different in his eyes. It wasn’t the tension that used to appear whenever he was about to reveal a problem, nor the quiet concern that had accompanied him during so many months. It was anticipation. An almost youthful anticipation, so out of place in a man who had spent his life trying to control every detail that Helena ended up smiling.

“All right.”

“All right what?”

“I trust you.”

His smile grew slightly wider.

“Then, at six.”

“If it’s a disguised meeting, I’m leaving.”

“It’s not a meeting.”

“Dinner with investors?”

“Not that either.”

“A family meeting?”

“Helena.”

She laughed.

“I’m just trying to prepare myself.”

Alexander leaned down and kissed her forehead.

“For the first time, you don’t need to prepare for anything.”

And he left before she could ask anything else.

For the rest of the day, Helena tried to concentrate on work, but curiosity eventually won. When she finally left the office, she found Alexander waiting in the car. He got out to open the door for her, a gesture he performed with such natural ease that it could still surprise her, and only returned to the driver’s seat after Helena had settled in.

“Can I know where we’re going now?”

“Not yet.”

“You’re enjoying this way too much.”

“A little.”

She watched the scenery through the window as they left the city center behind. After a few minutes, she realized she knew the route. The car was heading toward the old part of the city, where the historic buildings had undergone months of assessments, meetings, and restoration plans. Helena turned toward Alexander.

“Are you taking me to one of the properties from the project?”

“Maybe.”

“Alexander.”

“We’re almost there.”

She tried not to smile, but failed.

When the car finally stopped, Helena remained silent for a few seconds.

In front of them stood an old railway station, a building of simple, elegant architecture that had remained closed for years. Helena knew the place. It had been part of one of the first surveys for the revitalization project. During one of the first meetings, she had argued that the building should not be turned into just another commercial development. The original structure was too important to disappear behind a purely aesthetic renovation. She remembered spending hours discussing possibilities, talking about how the space could once again belong to the city.

But that was not what left her speechless.

The station was illuminated.

The doors were open.

And warm lights streamed through the restored windows, revealing an interior that had been completely transformed.

“What is this?” she asked, almost in a whisper.

Alexander got out of the car.

“Come with me.”

Helena followed him.

When she crossed the doorway, she stopped again.

The old hall had been restored while preserving its original details. The walls had been recovered, the stained-glass windows cleaned, and the wooden structure carefully restored. But what occupied the central space were not commercial tables or offices. There were shelves. Hundreds of them. Books filled the walls, arranged along wide, welcoming aisles. There were armchairs near the windows, small reading tables, warm lamps, and a children’s area at the back of the hall. In the center, a large circular table held books in different languages. Beside it, a discreet sign explained that the space would be open to the community free of charge, with rooms dedicated to reading, studying, literary gatherings, and language classes.

Helena stood motionless.

“Alexander...”

He stopped beside her.

“You once said that a city is only truly revitalized when people return to occupying the places they had learned to ignore.”

She slowly turned her face toward him.

“You remember that?”

“I remember almost everything you say.”

Helena looked back at the space.

“When did you do this?”

“We started working on it a few months ago.”

“A few months?”

“Before everything fell apart.”

She ran her fingers along the edge of one of the shelves.

“You knew?”

“I knew you liked this place. I knew it bothered you when they talked about turning the building into a commercial development. And I knew that whenever you talked about the project, this was the kind of space you were really talking about. A place that wouldn’t just increase property values, but give something back to the people.”

Helena felt her eyes fill with tears.

“You did this for me?”

Alexander took a moment before answering.

“I did it because I believe in what you believe. But I also did it because I wanted there to be a place in the city that reminded people of you, even if your name wasn’t on the door.”

She let out an emotional laugh.

“That is probably the most romantic thing anyone has ever done for me.”

“I was trying to impress you.”

“You succeeded.”

He took her hand.

“I’m not finished yet.”

Helena frowned.

“There’s more?”

Alexander led her through the hall. They walked between the shelves until they reached a glass door at the back. When he opened it, Helena found a small indoor garden that could not be seen from the street. There were young trees, wooden benches, and small tables scattered among plants and flowers. In the center stood a larger tree, surrounded by a circular wooden structure. Beneath it was a small plaque.

Helena approached.

She read it.

There was no name of Alexander.

No name of the Blackwood family.

Only a sentence:

“For all the days we still have ahead.”

She stood still before the plaque.

Alexander remained a few steps behind her without saying anything.

Helena ran her fingers over the letters.

“You put this here.”

“I did.”

“Why?”

He approached slowly.

“Because for a long time I thought loving someone meant trying to prevent anything bad from happening to that person. Then I understood that wasn’t it. Loving you doesn’t mean building a wall between you and the world. It means building a place we can return to after facing the world.”

Helena turned toward him.

Alexander was different from the man he had been that night when they first kissed. There was no fear in his face. No tension from someone already calculating every possible consequence. There was only a man standing before the woman he loved, without hidden documents, without threats waiting on the other side of a door, and without a decision being made by him alone.

“I don’t want to promise that I’ll never be afraid,” he continued. “I probably will be. I don’t want to promise that I’ll never make mistakes, because I know I will. But I want to promise that when it happens, you’ll know. I won’t disappear. I won’t decide on my own. I won’t try to love you in a way that leaves you outside.”

Helena felt a tear escape.

“Did you rehearse that?”

Alexander smiled.

“A few times.”

She laughed through her tears.

“I knew it.”

“I wanted to say it properly.”

“You did.”

He moved closer.

“One last thing.”

Helena looked at him suspiciously.

“You really like that phrase.”

“A little.”

Alexander took a small box from his pocket.

Helena froze.

He opened it.

Inside was a delicate ring, without extravagance, with a small stone surrounded by discreet details. It was not a piece of jewelry that shouted wealth or a surname. It was beautiful precisely because it seemed to have been chosen with her in mind.

Alexander took her hand.

“I don’t want to ask you to forget everything that happened. I don’t want you to look back and think that every difficult thing had to happen for us to get here. Some things were too painful for that. But I want you, when you think about what comes next, to know that I’m thinking about us.”

Helena looked at the ring.

Then at him.

“Alexander...”

“This isn’t a promise that everything will be perfect.”

She smiled.

“Good.”

“It’s a promise that I want to keep choosing you. Tomorrow. The day after tomorrow. On good days, on difficult days, when we’re tired, when we disagree, when you think I’m being unbearable...”

“Then you’re already prepared for a long life with me.”

He laughed.

“I’m trying.”

Helena ran her fingers over his hand.

“And what exactly are you asking?”

Alexander became serious again.

“If you want to build this life with me.”

She looked around. At the garden. At the library that had been born from a conversation he had kept in his memory. At the small tree that would continue to grow in that space over the years. At the man standing before her, who had finally learned that protecting her did not mean hiding the world from her, but remaining beside her within it.

Then she smiled.

“I do.”

Alexander closed his eyes for a moment, as if that single word had reached a place inside him that no professional victory had ever reached.

“Are you sure?”

Helena laughed.

“Are you giving me the opportunity to change my mind?”

“No.”

“Then stop asking.”

He slipped the ring onto her finger.

Then he held her hand with both of his and kissed her knuckles.

“I love you.”

“I love you too.”

Alexander pulled her close.

The kiss came slowly, without urgency, without fear of being interrupted, and without any need to hide what they felt. Helena wrapped her arms around his neck as he held her by the waist, and for a few seconds, all that existed was that moment.

They remained there for some time, embracing in the garden as night deepened over the city. For the first time, Helena felt no need to think about what would happen next. She did not need to look for hidden signs, interpret silences, or imagine what someone might try to take from them next. The future, for the first time, did not feel like a threat or a question. It simply felt like something they could build together, one day at a time.

Before leaving, Helena walked back toward the tree and touched the plaque with her fingertips.

“It will grow.”

Alexander stopped beside her.

“Yes.”

“And one day no one will remember that it was small.”

“Perhaps.”

Helena looked at him.

“We will remember.”

Alexander intertwined his fingers with hers.

“We will remember everything.”

She smiled.

“Even the bad things?”

He thought for a moment.

“Especially the things that taught us what not to repeat.”

Helena squeezed his hand.

Then they walked back through the illuminated hall, passing the shelves, the tables, and the windows open to the night. When they reached the door, she looked back one last time.

The space was empty.

But it did not feel abandoned.

For the first time, that place did not seem to hold the past.

It seemed to be waiting for the future.

Alexander opened the car door for her and, before Helena got in, held her hand.

“Helena.”

She turned.

“Yes?”

He smiled.

“Welcome to the rest of our story.”

She looked at him for a few seconds before smiling too.

“Finally.”

And she got into the car.

Alexander closed the door, walked around, and took the wheel. As they drove away, Helena leaned her head against the seat and watched the city lights pass by the window while the ring reflected tiny points of light across her hand.

This time, there were no questions waiting for answers.

No secrets hidden behind closed doors.

No distance between what they felt and what they had the courage to say.

There was only the road ahead of them, Alexander’s hand searching for hers over the console, and the quiet certainty that some stories do not end when they finally find their answers.

Some end when two people, after everything they have lived through, choose to keep writing together.
